questions.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the masses, in kilograms, of paper collected each week by two classes for a recycling drive.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Class}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline 8\text{B}&24&5\\ 8\text{F}&24&14\end{array}$
Which conclusion is best supported by the table?

options.text: The two classes collected the same amount per week on average, but $8$B was the more consistent.
$8$B collected more paper per week on average than $8$F.
options.why: Read the smaller range as a bigger total; the two means are both $24$ kg.

options.text: $8$F collected more paper per week on average, because its range is larger.
options.why: Treated the range as an amount collected rather than a measure of spread.

options.text: $8$F was the more consistent class, because its range is larger.
options.why: Reversed the rule: the smaller range, not the larger, means more consistent.

questions.solution_text:
$24 = 24$
The means are equal, so neither class collected more per week on average.
$5 < 14$
$8$B has the smaller range, so $8$B's weekly totals varied less.

options.text: More than twice as many students entered for Koala as for Dingo.
Half of all the entries came from Koala.
options.why: Took the tallest column to be half the total; $40$ out of $116$ is well under half.

options.text: Dingo has fewer students in it than any other house.
options.why: Read fewest entries as fewest students; the graph counts entries, not house sizes.

options.text: Every house entered at least $30$ students.
options.why: Overlooked the Dingo column, which reaches only $18$ entries.

questions.solution_text:
Koala reaches $40$ entries and Dingo reaches $18$ entries.
$2 \times 18 = 36$
$40 > 36$, so Koala's entries are more than double Dingo's.

questions.question_text: A school has $850$ students. All $22$ members of its debating club are asked whether the school should hold a public-speaking day, and $19$ of them say yes. Which conclusion does this data support?

options.text: Most members of the debating club want a public-speaking day.
Most of the $850$ students at the school want a public-speaking day.
options.why: Stretched a result about $22$ debaters to a school where nobody else was asked.

options.text: About $19$ out of every $22$ students at the school want a public-speaking day.
options.why: Applied the club's proportion to the school, though no non-members were surveyed.

options.text: No student outside the debating club wants a public-speaking day.
options.why: Counted students who were never asked as though they had answered no.

questions.solution_text:
Every one of the $22$ club members answered, so the data is a census of the debating club.
$19$ out of $22$ is more than half of the club.
Students outside the club were never asked, so the data describes the club only.

questions.question_text: A school put a second recycling bin in the playground at the start of Term $2$. The mean mass of recycling collected each week rose from $31$ kg in Term $1$ to $44$ kg in Term $2$. Which conclusion is best supported by this data?

options.text: More recycling was collected each week on average in Term $2$ than in Term $1$.
The extra bin caused the rise in the amount of recycling collected.
options.why: Assumed the one change noticed must be the cause; masses record what happened, not why.

options.text: Students cared more about the environment in Term $2$ than in Term $1$.
options.why: Concluded about attitudes, which the weekly masses never measured.

options.text: The mean mass collected each week will rise again in Term $3$.
options.why: Extended a past change into a term the data does not cover.

questions.solution_text:
$44 > 31$
The data records the mean mass collected each week in each term.
The means are all it measures, so the comparison of the two terms is the only conclusion it supports.

questions.question_text: All $95$ students in Year $8$ were asked which one activity they would choose on the class-project day. Cooking was chosen by $31$ students, more than any other activity. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: Cooking is the most chosen activity among Year $8$ students at the school.
Cooking is the most chosen activity among students at the school.
options.why: Extended a census of Year $8$ to year groups that were never asked.

options.text: Most Year $8$ students chose cooking.
options.why: Read 'more than any other' as 'more than half'; $31$ out of $95$ is under half.

options.text: About a third of all the students at the school chose cooking.
options.why: Applied Year $8$'s proportion to a whole school that was not surveyed.

questions.solution_text:
Every one of the $95$ Year $8$ students answered, so the data is a census of Year $8$.
$31$ is a larger count than any other activity received.
A census gives the exact result for its population, which here is Year $8$ alone.

questions.question_text: $60$ of the $500$ students at a school are chosen at random and asked how many library books they borrowed last term. The mean is $6.5$ books and the range is $19$ books. Which conclusion does this data support?

options.text: Students at the school borrowed about $6.5$ books each last term.
Every student at the school borrowed about $6.5$ books last term.
options.why: Read a mean as a value each student had; a range of $19$ shows they varied widely.

options.text: Exactly $6.5$ books were borrowed per student across the school.
options.why: Treated an estimate from $60$ students as an exact figure for all $500$.

options.text: The most common number of books borrowed was $6.5$ books.
options.why: Confused the mean with the mode, which this data does not give.

questions.solution_text:
The $60$ students were chosen at random from all $500$, so the sample fairly represents the school.
A sample gives an estimate, so the conclusion must be written as an approximate value.
The sample mean of $6.5$ books is that estimate.

questions.question_text:
A school wants to know how many of its $600$ students would buy a new canteen breakfast.
Study $1$: $40$ students chosen at random from the school roll are asked, and $14$ say yes.
Study $2$: the first $40$ students in the canteen queue at recess are asked, and $31$ say yes.
Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: About $14$ out of every $40$ students at the school would buy the breakfast, from Study $1$.
About $31$ out of every $40$ students at the school would buy the breakfast, from Study $2$.
options.why: Chose the larger figure, though Study 2's sample came only from canteen customers.

options.text: About $45$ out of every $80$ students at the school would buy the breakfast, from both studies.
options.why: Pooled the two samples, carrying Study 2's canteen-queue over-estimate into the total.

options.text: Neither study supports a conclusion, because $40$ students is only part of the school.
options.why: Assumed a sample never supports a conclusion; a random sample supports an estimate.

questions.solution_text:
Study $1$ chose its $40$ students at random from the whole roll, so every student had the same chance of being picked.
Study $2$ asked only students already in the canteen queue, who are the students most likely to buy canteen food.
Only Study $1$'s sample represents the school, so only its result can be used as an estimate for the $600$ students.

options.text: More books were borrowed in Week $6$ than in any earlier week.
Borrowing increased in every week of the term.
options.why: Ignored the falls in Week 3 and Week 5; the graph goes up and down.

options.text: More than $350$ books will be borrowed in Week $7$.
options.why: Extended the graph into a week the data does not cover.

options.text: The new displays are what lifted the borrowing figures.
options.why: Gave a cause for the rise; the graph records totals only, never reasons.

questions.solution_text:
Week $6$ is the highest point on the graph, at $300$ books.
Every earlier week is lower, the next highest being Week $4$ at $250$ books.
The graph falls from $200$ to $175$ at Week $3$ and from $250$ to $225$ at Week $5$, so borrowing did not rise every week.
